bottleneck: Writing whole synthetic genomes — yeast's 16 chromosomes were a landmark — requires assembling millions of bases with near-zero error, then booting the genome in a living cell. Debugging a non-viable synthetic genome means searching megabases for a lethal design flaw with poor diagnostic tools, since failures give little clue about their location. Scaling this from yeast to plants or mammals multiplies complexity beyond current capacity, as genome size, repeat content, and epigenetic requirements all explode.
current_state: Synthetic yeast (Sc2.0) nears completion after a decade-plus international effort. No synthetic multicellular genome exists; mammalian synthetic chromosomes remain distant.
title: Whole-genome synthesis stuck at single-celled scale
why_it_blocks: Fully designed genomes would let us build organisms from specifications — crops, cell factories, model systems. The debugging bottleneck keeps that future at microbial scale while the most valuable applications need multicellular hosts.
